The {{Nihongo|'''Defense Intelligence Headquarters'''|情報本部|Jōhōhonbu}}<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.cas.go.jp/jp/seisaku/hourei/name.pdf |title= 部局課名・官職名英訳名称一覧 |trans-title= Names of Government Organizations and Positions |access-date=June 9, 2008}}</ref> is a [[military intelligence]] and [[signal intelligence]] agency of the [[Government of Japan|Japanese government]], under the jurisdiction of the [[Japan]]ese [[Ministry of Defense (Japan)|Ministry of Defense]]. It is currently one of the biggest Japanese intelligence agencies.<ref name="History">{{cite web|url=http://andreworos.washcoll.edu/password/oros_ijic_0102.pdf |title=Japan's Growing Intelligence Capabilities |author= Andrew Oros |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20090320155104/http://andreworos.washcoll.edu/password/oros_ijic_0102.pdf |archive-date=2009-03-20 |access-date=June 9, 2008 }}</ref> The DIH was modeled after the American [[Defense Intelligence Agency]].<ref name="Report">{{Cite news|url=https://nautilus.org/napsnet/napsnet-daily-report/napsnet-daily-report-24-january-1997/|archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20190523120653/https://nautilus.org/napsnet/napsnet-daily-report/napsnet-daily-report-24-january-1997/|archive-date = 2019-05-23|title = NAPSNet Daily Report 24 January, 1997 &#124; Nautilus Institute for Security and Sustainability|newspaper = Nautilus Institute for Security and Sustainability &#124; We Hold That It is Possible to Build Peace, Create Security, and Restore Sustainability for All People in Our Time|date = 24 January 1997}}</ref>

==History==
[[File:DIH_facilities_in_Japan.png|thumb|DIH facilities in Japan]]

Back in the 1980s, the former [[Ministry of Defense (Japan)|Defense Agency]] had several intelligence divisions with different duties. Among these intelligence divisions in the Defense Agency had included those from the Central Data Command Unit, the Joint Staff Council's Second Office and the three branches from the chiefs of staff in the [[Japan Self-Defense Forces]] (JSDF).<ref name="DIH">{{Cite web |title=Defence Intelligence Headquarters (DIH) |url=https://www.globalsecurity.org/intell/world/japan/dih.htm |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200111105700/https://www.globalsecurity.org/intell/world/japan/dih.htm |archive-date=2020-01-11}}</ref> Most of the DIH's establishment was based on the Annex Chamber (or Special Annex),{{Sfnp|Samuels|2019|p=110}}  Second Intelligence Division, Ground Staff Office.{{Sfnp|Williams|2021|p=133}}  
They collected signals from the [[Sino–Soviet border conflict]] of 1969 and the [[Soviet Afghan war]] of 1979.<ref name="auto">{{Cite web|url=https://www.eastasiaforum.org/2021/08/26/japans-five-eyes-chance-and-challenge/|title=Japan's Five Eyes chance and challenge|date=August 26, 2021|website=East Asia Forum}}</ref>
They were also involved in intercepting communications that led to and after the shooting of [[Korean Air Lines Flight 007]] through the Wakkanai Station.<ref name="Report"/>

A supposed plan to integrate the intelligence divisions of the three [[Japan Self-Defense Forces|JSDF]] branches started in 1988 before lack of cooperation and subordination ended it.<ref name="DIH"/>

Plans to consolidate all the intelligence bureaus of the old Defense Administration into one agency had started in the 1990s<ref>{{Cite web |date=December 25, 2019 |title=Japan, Intelligence and Security |url=<!-- do not turn into archive, the actual url is blocked by wikipedia --> https://web.archive.org/web/20191225205914/http://www.faqs.org/espionage//Int-Ke/Japan-Intelligence-and-Security.html |archive-url=<!-- --> |archive-date=<!-- -->}}</ref> after the [[National Diet]] had passed a law in May 1996, calling for the creation of a central military intelligence agency before the DIH was eventually established on January 20, 1997<ref name="Report"/><ref name="Agency">{{Cite web |title=Defence Intelligence Headquarters |url=https://fas.org/irp/world/japan/dih.htm |access-date=June 9, 2008}}</ref> after intelligence units from the JSDF, Japanese Defense Agency and the Joint Staff council are united<ref>{{Cite web |title=&#91;INDONESIA-P&#93; CSM - Asia Eyes New J |url=http://www.hamline.edu/apakabar/basisdata/1997/03/21/0017.html |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20041108015922/http://www.hamline.edu/apakabar/basisdata/1997/03/21/0017.html |archive-date=2004-11-08}}</ref> with  the appointment of [[Lieutenant General]] Kunimi Masahiro as the agency's first commanding officer.<ref name="History"/>

Initially, DIH civilian and military staff members were numbered at 1,580<ref name="Agency"/> with a planned manpower of 2,000 personnel<ref>{{Cite web |title=Press Conference by the Press Secretary |url=https://fas.org/irp/world/japan/528.htm |access-date=June 9, 2008}}</ref> before it reached its current manpower of 2,300 staff members.<ref name="Paper">{{Cite web |title=Operations of Self-Defense Forces for Defense of Japan, Disaster Relief and Civil Protection |url=http://www.mod.go.jp/e/publ/w_paper/pdf/2006/3-1-1.pdf |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110930142605/http://www.mod.go.jp/e/publ/w_paper/pdf/2006/3-1-1.pdf |archive-date=2011-09-30}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |title=Current State of Intelligence and Intelligence Issue in Japan |url=http://www.nids.go.jp/english/dissemination/briefing/2006/pdf/100.pdf |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20080625185434/http://www.nids.go.jp/english/dissemination/briefing/2006/pdf/100.pdf |archive-date=2008-06-25}}</ref> In 2011, the manpower is 1,907 members<ref>{{Cite web |title=Defense Programs and Budget of Japan |url=http://www.mod.go.jp/e/d_budget/pdf/231220.pdf |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20130214001823/http://www.mod.go.jp/e/d_budget/pdf/231220.pdf |archive-date=2013-02-14}}</ref>

[[Spy satellites]] had been planned for launch in 1998 in order to augment the DIH's intelligence gathering capabilities. Though two were able to launch into space, two more were destroyed in a botched attempt to send them to space.<ref>{{Cite web |title=With Eyes Wide Shut: Japan, Heisei Militarization and the Bush Doctrine |url=http://nautilus.rmit.edu.au/publications/japanese-militarization.html |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20091013080104/http://nautilus.rmit.edu.au/publications/japanese-militarization.html |archive-date=13 October 2009 |access-date=11 January 2022 |website=nautilus.rmit.edu.au}}</ref>

In 2005, the DIH suffered its first internal leak of classified information when a [[Colonel]] in the JASDF was arrested for allegedly leaking information regarding an accident involving a [[People's Liberation Army Navy]] [[Submarine]] that took place that same year in the [[South China Sea]].<ref>{{Cite web |date=7 April 2008 |title=The secrets of the sea |url=http://www.japantimes.co.jp/opinion/2008/04/07/editorials/the-secrets-of-the-sea |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160410173058/http://www.japantimes.co.jp/opinion/2008/04/07/editorials/the-secrets-of-the-sea |archive-date=2016-04-10}}</ref>

The DIH announced in 2006 that a liaison office had been established in [[Washington, D.C.]], with the [[National Security Agency]].<ref>{{Cite web |title=29 Sept 2006 news feed |url=http://www.space-library.com/060929MS.pdf |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20111004090025/http://www.space-library.com/060929MS.pdf |archive-date=2011-10-04 |website=space-library.com}}</ref>

By FY 2027, the DIH plans to use AI to automate intelligence collection through OSINT and future forecast functions.<ref name="Slide"/>

===Known activities===
* After a [[North Korea]]n [[Taepodong-1|Taepodong-1 ballistic missile]] had been launched on August 31, 1998, [[Japan Self-Defense Forces|JSDF]] ships and aircraft began to search the [[Sea of Japan]] to collect any debris of the missile with the DIH providing intelligence support such as dispatching [[North Korea]]n specialists to the [[United States]] over the matter.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Section 2. Response of the Defense Agency to the Missile Launch by North Korea |url=http://www.globalsecurity.org/wmd/library/news/dprk/1999/td-1-japan99.htm |access-date=June 16, 2008}}</ref>
* [[North Korea]]n radio communications were intercepted by the SIGINT division's Kikaijima, Kagoshima radio monitoring station. The successful interception of [[North Korea]]n communications later led to a [[Battle of Amami-Ōshima|naval shootout]] between ships of the [[Japan Coast Guard]] and a suspected [[North Korea]]n spy boat in 2001 near the island of [[Amami-Ōshima]] before the latter had been destroyed.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Japan's Secret SIGINT Organizations: Focusing On North Korea |url=http://www.popular-communications.com/March%2007%20PC%20Highlights.html |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20080317193032/http://www.popular-communications.com/March+07+PC+Highlights.html |archive-date=2008-03-17 |access-date=June 15, 2008}}</ref>
* The DIH had provided intelligence to JGSDF forces that were deployed in [[Indonesia]] during the [[2006 Yogyakarta earthquake]].<ref name="Paper"/>
* Using a [[signals intelligence]] facility in [[Tachiarai]], the DIH reportedly monitor communications from transiting satellites for Cybersecurity as part of a program codenamed MALLARD.<ref name="intercept">{{Cite news |last=Gallagher |first=Ryan |date=May 19, 2018 |title=The Untold Story of Japan's Secret Spy Agency |url=https://theintercept.com/2018/05/19/japan-dfs-surveillance-agency |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180521231622/https://theintercept.com/2018/05/19/japan-dfs-surveillance-agency |archive-date=May 21, 2018}}</ref> The program reportedly intercepts more than 12 million Internet communications per day.<ref name="intercept"/>
*In May 2019, several Chinese JH7 fighter-bombers conducted a training exercise over the high seas of the East China Sea, using a JMSDF destroyer as a target for attack. The JSDF side is said to have intercepted radio transmissions emitted by the Chinese warplanes stating that they were training to attack the Maritime Self-Defense Force ships as targets.<ref>{{cite web | url=https://www.zakzak.co.jp/article/20190819-BZGDLGXRTVP7BOSERFWIE5QL2U/?outputType=amp| title=中国軍機が海自艦を標的に危険訓練、一触即発の事態に！ 日本側は冷静対応も…政府関係者「いざというときには強く出る」| date=18 August 2019}}</ref>

==Command==
The DIH is under the jurisdiction of the Joint Staff and is controlled by the Defense Intelligence Committee, which is made up of the Chiefs of Staff of the JGSDF, JMSDF and JASDF along with the Chief of Staff, Joint Staff, State Minister of Defense and the [[Minister of Defense (Japan)|Minister of Defense]].<ref name="Gaiyo">{{Cite web|url=http://www.mod.go.jp/dih/gaiyou.html|archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20181005154101/http://www.mod.go.jp/dih/gaiyou.html|archive-date = 2018-10-05|title = 防衛省・自衛隊：防衛省ウェブサイトのＨｔｔｐｓへの切り替えのお知らせ}}</ref><ref name=Japan2007>{{cite web |title=Japan Primer |publisher=University of Texas |year=2007 |url=http://www1.apan-info.net/Portals/45/VIC_Products/2007/04/070403-P-Japan-web.doc |access-date=2007-10-06 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20080625185434/http://www1.apan-info.net/Portals/45/VIC_Products/2007/04/070403-P-Japan-web.doc |archive-date=2008-06-25 }}</ref>

Command of the DIH was given directly to the [[Minister of Defense (Japan)|Japanese Minister of Defense]] in March 2006.<ref name="Paper"/> The deputy officer is usually a civilian officially appointed by the MOD.<ref name="STIMSON">{{cite web|url=https://www.stimson.org/sites/default/files/file-attachments/Tatsumi_%20Japan%27s_Security_Policy_Infrastructure_Final_Version.pdf|title=JAPAN'S NATIONAL SECURITY POLICY INFRASTRUCTURE - CAN TOKYO MEET WASHINGTON'S EXPECTATION?|archiveurl=https://web.archive.org/web/20191223084217/https://www.stimson.org/sites/default/files/file-attachments/Tatsumi_%20Japan%27s_Security_Policy_Infrastructure_Final_Version.pdf|archivedate=2019-12-23|publisher=Stimson Center|author=Yuki Tatsumi|accessdate=2019-12-13}}</ref> Four Defense Intelligence Officers (DIOs) are also appointed with three being colonels from the JGSDF or the JASDF with one a civilian official.<ref name="STIMSON"/>

The SIGINT facilities managed by the Chobetsu (Chosa Besshitsu) or the Annex Chamber, Second Section, Second Investigation Division in English, from 1958 to 1997, is currently managed by the DIH.<ref>{{Cite web | url=https://nautilus.org/wp-content/uploads/2015/08/Japan-SIGINT-Ground-Stations-online.pdf | title=Japan’s Signals Intelligence (SIGINT) Ground Stations: A Visual Guide | website=nautilus.org}}</ref> Command of the SIGINT division is usually filled by a senior officer appointed by the NPA from the Prefectural Police.<ref>{{cite web | url=https://dailynk.jp/archives/60171/4 | title=【対北情報戦の内幕-13-】自衛隊が「工作船接近」を知りながら拉致事件を見逃した理由 | date=23 January 2016 }}</ref><ref>Dover, Goodman and Hillebrand, page 203</ref>

A number of divisions were established under the DIH, including the following:<ref name=Japan2007/><ref name="Gaiyou">{{Cite web|url=http://www.mod.go.jp/dih/gaiyou.html|archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20090418165548/http://www.mod.go.jp/dih/gaiyou.html|archive-date = 2009-04-18|title = 防衛省・自衛隊：防衛省ウェブサイトのＨｔｔｐｓへの切り替えのお知らせ}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.mod.go.jp/dih/organization.html|title=情報本部の組織|website=www.mod.go.jp}}</ref>

==Role==
The main role of the DIH is to collect information and analyse for planning defense and operation policy. The agency collect information from open sources, signals and image intelligence as well as from other [[Government of Japan|Japanese government]] ministries, [[Japan]]ese embassies and other affiliated ministries and organizations.<ref name="Paper"/><ref name="Gaiyou"/> In addition, they also gather intelligence through surveillance activities.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.mod.go.jp/e/publ/w_paper/pdf/2007/30Part2_Chap3_Sec3.pdf |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170322181221/https://www.mod.go.jp/e/publ/w_paper/pdf/2007/30Part2_Chap3_Sec3.pdf |archive-date=2017-03-22 |title=Section 3 Organization of the MOD/SDF}}</ref>

The analysis results are reported and shared with the Prime Minister, the Minister of Defense, internal departments and other organizations of the Ministry of Defense, [[National Security Council (Japan)]] and other relevant ministries and agencies, and units of the Ground, Maritime, and Air Self-Defense Forces for use in policy decisions and unit operations.

In addition, in the National Defense Strategy approved by the Cabinet in December 2022, the DIH is expected to play a central role in information warfare in the defense of Japan, in addition to its existing role.<ref name="Slide"/>

It is not allowed to obtain non-military intelligence in Japan or information from cyberspace.<ref name="auto"/>

==Seal==
The seal of the DIH consist of the following symbols:
* [[Pheasant]] – Quality of intelligence gathering at high speed<ref name="Symbol">{{Cite web|url=http://www.mod.go.jp/dih/symbol.html|archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20070714144058/http://www.mod.go.jp/dih/symbol.html|archive-date = 2007-07-14|title = 防衛省・自衛隊：防衛省ウェブサイトのＨｔｔｐｓへの切り替えのお知らせ}}</ref>
* Red [[oval]] shapes around [[Earth]] – Positions of [[spy satellites]]<ref name="Symbol" />
* [[Lightning]] – Radio waves<ref name="Symbol" />
* [[Star]] – Section and Stations of the DIH<ref name="Symbol" />

==Known DIH directors==
DIH directors are usually positioned by a Lieutenant General from the JGSDF/JASDF or a Vice Admiral from the JMSDF.

* Fumio Ota<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.sandiegouniontribune.com/uniontrib/20071216/news_1n16missile.html |title=U.S. To aid Japan with defensive missile test &#124; the San Diego Union-Tribune |website=www.sandiegouniontribune.com |access-date=11 January 2022 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160305075112/http://www.sandiegouniontribune.com/uniontrib/20071216/news_1n16missile.html |archive-date=5 March 2016 |url-status=dead}}</ref>
* Kenichiro Hokazono; the former Chief of Air Staff
* Koji Shimohira
* {{Nihongo3|Tadashi Miyagawa|宮川正}}
